newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Iran aims to raise oil profile in Asia - minister.
newsitem.headline: Iran aims to raise oil profile in Asia - minister.

text.p: Iran aims to raise its presence in Asia through increased crude sales and direct direct investment in refinery upgrading projects, Vice Petroleum Minister Ghanimi Fard said on Tuesday.
The move through state-owned National Iranian Oil Co (NIOC) had already made inroads in China, he told Reuters in an interview.
"We are ready to cooperate with all those who are seriously concerned about the security of future energy supply to Asia," he said.
Iran exports nearly 40 percent of its crude to Asia compared to a high of 62.6 percent in 1970.
"There is no reason why this share cannot increase to its earlier level given Iranian political stability, expertise and massive reserves," Fard said.
Iranian crude oil exports in May were around 2.28 million barrels per day (bpd), down from 2.55 in April.

Fard said compared to some Middle East countries such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, which export in excess of 80 percent of their crude to Asia, Iran's lower export exposure to the region would allow it to raise supplies easily if needed.

Iran's move to expand in Asia is most advanced in China where, following a visit by Oil Minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh in May, several several deals were sealed for both upstream and downstream activities.
The two countries agreed to form a joint-venture company to explore for offshore oil and gas in Iran, China and in third countries, Fard said.
"We have decided to have a joint-venture working on the offshore both in Iranian and China and third countries," he said.
Fard said the new company would be owned jointly owned by China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) and NIOC. He said the new venture had not identified any specific area for immediate development.
Iran had also sealed an agreement with state-owened Chinese refiner Sinopec to revamp an oil refinery in southern China.
Fard said that would allow the refinery to process more Iranian crude and cost US$250 million.
The upgrade will allow the refinery to raise its use of Iranian crude from the existing 20,000 barrel per day, he said.
Iran and China have agreed to raise Chinese import of Iranian crude to 200,000 bpd in the year 2000 from the current 70,000 bpd, Fard said.
He said Iran would consider similar investments in other older refineries in Asia which will guarantee crude purchase.
Fard said Iran was also hoping to raise its oil product share in the Asian market following the start up of its Bandar Abbas refinery next month.
The 232,000-bpd refinery would be able to produce high quality gas oil and kerosene that will meet new regulations in Asia, he said.
